name: deep
label: DEEP — military & tech mysteries
description: Submarines, spy missions, lost aircraft, rockets and the machines behind them, told in teal and orange: real archive footage in a dark monitor with a timecode, stencilled datelines over the picture, an abstract route chart of the journey, a cutaway of the vessel with the crew as glowing figures and the ones the story follows in red, a sonar screen of contacts, a classified readout of the facts, the wall map of a headquarters the camera pushes into, two-tone maps with a white route, and pictures drawn as matte 3D renders where no footage exists. No captions.
tagline: Teal and orange: stencil dates, sonar, cutaways, the map room.
cost: about $0.03 a minute with the Gemini free tier (voice + cutouts); about $0.30 a minute when footage is watched on paid credits

look.still_suffix: Rendered as a matte 3D animation still: clean physically based materials, soft volumetric light, a teal-and-charcoal palette with one orange accent, deep shadows, a slight depth of field, cinematic 16:9 framing, no text, no watermark, no logo, no lens flare.
look.options_note: DEEP: real archive footage in a dark monitor, stencil datelines, sonar, cutaways, readouts, the map room, two-tone maps, and matte 3D renders drawn where no footage exists. No captions by default.

pacing.hook_notes: This is a military or technical mystery: the first minute opens on a stencil (the date or the place of the cold open), a map (two-tone) on the first place, a cutaway of the vessel, aircraft, rocket or station the story is about the first time it is named, a readout of the mission's facts within the first 40 seconds, a spotlight on the first public person named, and text labels for depths, distances, speeds and dates.
pacing.body_notes: After the hook: archive footage in the monitor carries it; a route when a journey or a distance is described; a sonar when contacts, detection or pursuit are described; a cutaway when the story goes inside a machine; a readout for any list of specifications or facts; a maproom when a plan, an operation or a headquarters is described; a stencil on every new date; a map when the story moves; a spotlight on each new public person. One graphic every 20 to 30 seconds, never the same twice in a row.

prompts.outline:
You are the head writer of a channel about military and technological mysteries — submarines that vanished, spy operations under the sea, aircraft that never landed, rockets, radar, cables, codes — told like a classified file read aloud.

TITLE: [INSERT TITLE HERE]
LENGTH: [INSERT LENGTH — e.g., 15 minutes, 20 minutes, 25 minutes]

Plan the episode in plain prose, as numbered beats of about one minute each, in causal or chronological order.
- Everything is real: real vessels with their names and numbers, real operations, real dates, real depths, distances, speeds and crews, real officers and engineers. Use only facts you are certain of; round what is disputed or classified and say "around" or "reportedly".
- Beat 1 is a cold open on the most dramatic real moment — the last message, the contact on the sonar, the dive, the launch — with the date, the place and one number, then the question the story turns on.
- Every beat names what can be drawn or shown: the machine (so a cutaway can be built), the route (so a chart can be drawn), the contacts, the headquarters, the specifications, the places on a map, the archive footage that exists.
- Explain how the technology worked, plainly, at the moment the story needs it — one mechanism per beat at most.
- Every few beats a turn: what they expected, what actually happened. Keep one revelation for the last third.
- The last beat lands what was found, what is still unknown, or what the mission changed, and returns to the image of the cold open.
For each beat, write the facts it states and the things on screen that carry them.
prompts.script:
Write the complete narration for this file from the plan below.

THE PLAN:
[INSERT OUTLINE HERE]

HOW IT SOUNDS
- A deep, unhurried narrator with the authority of someone who has read the declassified pages. Short sentences. Present tense for the operation, past tense for background. Fragments at the turns: "Four hundred feet. Then silence."
- The first words are the cold open: a date, a place and a number, in the middle of the most dramatic moment.
- Every sentence carries something the file can show: a vessel, a place, a date, a depth, a distance, a name, a mechanism.
- Say numbers and dates the way they are read aloud ("October nineteen seventy-one", "twelve hundred kilometres", "three hundred and sixty feet"), never digits or symbols.
- Explain the technology in one clear sentence when the story needs it, never as a lecture.
- Real facts only. No invented dialogue, no invented figures; classified details are said as "reportedly" or "around".
- Plain spoken text only: no headings, no stage directions, no speaker labels, no lists.
- A question the viewer wants answered every minute or so, answered soon after.
- Never say "in this video". End on what was found or what remains unknown, back at the image of the cold open; then one short line asking viewers to subscribe for the next file.

thumbnail.brief: A matte 3D-render-style scene in deep teal: the vessel, aircraft or machine of the story half in shadow, one orange accent (a light, a marking, a map), volumetric light. Two to four words of headline in a condensed stencil face, pale cyan, top-left, one word in orange. No faces, no arrows, no emoji.
